title: From Process Maps to Attention Maps: Transformer Architectures Versus Process Mining for Learning Trajectories in FLOSS Repositories
content: Learning in Free/Libre Open Source Software (FLOSS) communities has so far been analysed with ontologies, a-priori learning models and process mining, which yield process maps that an analyst can read. Neural sequence architectures, and the Transformer in particular, now dominate the modelling of event sequences, yet their value for FLOSS learning analytics has not been established. This paper compares the two traditions on a common footing. From 37 OpenStack repositories we construct a pseudonymised, developer-centred event log of 182,140 accepted contributions by 6512 developers (2010–2026), abstracted into eleven learning activities, and evaluate process-mining predictors, feature-based classifiers, an LSTM and a Transformer encoder on two tasks. In predicting a developer’s next activity, the Transformer (45.7% accuracy) improves on the best transition system (44.8%), but a single-layer LSTM performs better (47.0%) and is more robust when tested on later cohorts. In identifying future sustained contributors from their first three contributions, the LSTM reaches an AUROC of 0.664 and the Transformer 0.634, whereas a classifier built on directly-follows graphs remains close to chance (0.513). Attention turns out to be almost uniform over a developer’s history, and restricting it to the last four events costs nothing. Its rollout explanations rank activities as the interpretable models do (Spearman ρ = 0.75), but only process maps and regression coefficients show clearly that newcomers who contribute in quick succession and move from documentation into code are more likely to stay. We conclude that, at the scale of FLOSS learning logs, self-attention is a competitive but not a dominant architecture, and that process mining should remain the explanatory layer against which neural predictors are checked.
